claim: The requirement says that if T carries MessagePack attributes, they are honoured, and that contractless mode applies only when T has no [DataContract] or [MessagePackObject]. The change does not do this. Without a surrogate, Collect always calls CreateContractlessMembers, which never reads T's attributes. As a result: [MessagePackObject] types lose their integer [Key] layout and fall back to name-based string keys; [IgnoreMember] members are still serialized; [DataContract]/[DataMember] names and membership are ignored; and [Union] on T is unsupported (README limitation). This both breaks wire compatibility and leaks ignored members.

claim: In contractless mode, public get-only properties and readonly fields are dropped (IsPublicReadWrite filter), and types with only a parameterized constructor are rejected. The requirement asks for 'contractless behaviour over public members'. ContractlessStandardResolver serializes get-only members and deserializes through a matching constructor, so immutable referenced types silently lose data or cannot be formatted.

claim: The requirement says MessagePack attributes on T must be honoured. When no SurrogateType is set, `Collect` always calls `CreateContractlessMembers(type)`, and that method never reads T's attributes. Two inputs show the problem. First, a referenced `[MessagePackObject] class AnnotatedType { [Key(0)] int Visible; [IgnoreMember] int IgnoredSecret; }` still has `IgnoredSecret` serialized. Second, T's integer `[Key]` indexes are discarded: the type is written as a string-keyed map (alphabetical by name) instead of an array. `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]` are ignored in the same way.

On head the text contains IgnoredSecret and uses WriteMapHeader rather than WriteArrayHeader.

claim: `IsPartial` only checks the formatter's own declaration. The FormatterTemplate/StringKeyFormatterTemplate now emit the user formatter through `EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces` with `Formatter = new QualifiedNamedTypeName(formatter)`. As a result, a formatter nested in a non-partial containing class (`public class Outer { [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] internal partial class PayloadFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<Payload> {} }`) passes validation. The generator then emits code that does not compile (CS0260 missing partial on Outer, or CS0535 unimplemented members) instead of reporting MsgPack019.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterLogicReceipts.FormatterNestedInNonPartialTypeIsDiagnosedInsteadOfEmittingBrokenCode. It runs the generator on a nested formatter in a non-partial Outer and asserts that either an MsgPack diagnostic is reported or the output compilation has no errors. On head there is no MsgPack diagnostic and the output has compile errors.

claim: GeneratedFormatterCollector.GetInstanceMembers walks the base type chain and CreateMember sets DeclaringType = null, so members inherited from a base class are generated. Contractless mode also produces string keys sorted ordinally, while the dynamic ContractlessStandardResolver orders by declaration. A user who later switches between the dynamic and generated formatters would see different map layouts and member sets. Also, the contractless mode here skips get-only members, which ContractlessStandardResolver includes.

GeneratorUtilities now excludes any class that has the attribute from the hand-written formatter list. The exclusion happens even when the class is rejected (not partial, wrong interface) and produces no model. As a result the formatter silently drops out of the resolver too, but only for users who opted in with the new attribute, so the impact is limited.

claim: Contractless mode generates a formatter for ANY accessible type T, including types with sensitive or non-serializable members. Generated code is not subject to MessagePackSecurity differences, but the string-key path deserializes via the generated formatter with `new T()`, bypassing constructor validation of T. This is inherent to the feature and not a regression, but no depth-guard is verified: confirm the generated Deserialize still calls `options.Security.DepthStep(ref reader)` for the user-declared formatter path.

claim: The test only asserts that the generated formatter is registered and round-trips with default options. No test covers a [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] class that has no body and whose type is declared in a separate assembly with the output actually emitted; however the ExecutionTests do this. The missing piece is the negative case: the IsUserDeclaredFormatter flag in the template is never tested for the false path alongside it, but the existing snapshot tests cover that. A real gap is the GeneratorUtilities exclusion guard: if it were removed, the formatter would be registered twice, and no test checks for duplicate registration or for compile errors beyond the IsType assertion.

claim: Classes with [GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] are now excluded from the hand-written formatter set, which is what TypeCollector uses as KnownFormatters/custom-formatter precedence. If T is declared in the same compilation with [MessagePackObject], TypeCollector no longer sees that T has a custom formatter. It therefore also generates its own formatter for T, and the resolver registers two ObjectSerializationInfos for the same DataType: the user's formatter and the generated <T>Formatter. On base, a hand-written formatter suppressed the generated one.
